splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA's statutory measurement date for withdrawal liability requires all actuarial assumptions to be locked in by that date or allows actuaries to select assumptions afterward. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be determined as of the statutory measurement date and cannot be selected or changed after that date.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as the statute only requires that the assumptions be applied to data as of that date.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during periods of absconding, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release runs continuously regardless of absconding because no statute authorizes tolling, and courts lack authority to create common-law doctrines that extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim they previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than the separate requirements in § 2255(h). The split has persisted for years and affects access to collateral review for federal prisoners.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring relitigation of claims previously presented.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates can establish Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome determines whether challenges to mail-in voting deadlines and other election administration practices can proceed before elections or must wait until afterward, with significant implications for election litigation nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election because vote dilution or competitive injury from allegedly unlawful ballots constitutes a cognizable injury in fact.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates lack Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election because the alleged injury is too speculative or generalized before votes are actually counted.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether lenity trumps Auer/Kisor deference to agency interpretations in criminal contexts. At least three circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference, while others (including the Third Circuit) have held that agency deference trumps lenity. The Supreme Court's decision in Loper Bright overruling Chevron has cast further doubt on deference-first approaches.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations of ambiguous criminal provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through delegated interpretive power.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that deference to the Sentencing Commission's or agency's interpretation of ambiguous provisions takes precedence over the rule of lenity in criminal sentencing contexts.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), or whether possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. The split affects mandatory minimum sentencing for drug offenses and leads to disparate outcomes depending on geography.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as disjunctive or distributive in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' commentary (Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and attempt as 'controlled substance offenses' is a valid interpretation of § 4B1.2(b) entitled to deference under Stinson, or whether it impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its unambiguous text. The split has deepened following Kisor v. Wilkie's narrowing of Auer deference.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative and valid interpretation of the career-offender guideline, and that inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses under § 4B1.2(b).

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, and the commentary cannot expand the definition beyond what the text provides, especially after Kisor narrowed deference to agency interpretations.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Tuan Ngoc Mai

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the underlying substance is controlled under state but not federal law.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance to be federally scheduled or whether any state-controlled substance qualifies. The Eighth Circuit holds there is no federal-law limitation, while other circuits require the substance to be federally controlled.

positions.label: State-controlled substance suffices
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b)'s reference to 'an offense under state law' includes offenses involving substances controlled only under state law, with no requirement that the substance also be federally scheduled.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a controlled substance offense only if the substance is also controlled under federal law, reading the Guidelines in light of the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), may be considered as an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply divided on whether courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law — alone or in combination with other factors — as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. Some circuits permit it, while others hold that non-retroactive changes cannot contribute to such a finding. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) attempted to authorize it, but some circuits have held the Commission exceeded its authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as one factor in evaluating extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, particularly for unusually long sentences resulting from stacked § 924(c) convictions.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot be considered
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must bring challenges to the conditions or terms of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) exclusively through habeas corpus, or whether they may also use civil rights actions such as Bivens or § 1983.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging conditions of confinement that arguably affect the duration of their imprisonment, or whether civil rights actions remain available. The Supreme Court has noted but not resolved this question, which affects challenges to BOP decisions regarding First Step Act time credits, transfers, and other conditions.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for duration-related claims
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to the fact or duration of confinement — including BOP decisions about time credits and prerelease custody — must be brought exclusively through habeas corpus and not through civil rights actions.

positions.label: Conditions claims may proceed outside habeas
positions.summary: Holds that certain challenges to conditions of confinement or BOP administrative decisions may be brought through civil rights actions even when they overlap with habeas, as the Supreme Court left this question open in Preiser.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly consider punishment as a purpose of sentencing at supervised release revocation hearings under 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether punishment is a permissible sentencing purpose at supervised release revocation. The Sixth Circuit allows courts to expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, placing it at the extreme of a split. Other circuits hold that the purpose of revocation sentencing is limited to sanctioning the breach of trust and deterring future violations, not punishing the underlying violation.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider punishment as a purpose when sentencing at supervised release revocation, based on the statutory factors applicable at revocation.

positions.label: Punishment is not the purpose
positions.summary: Holds that revocation of supervised release is not meant to punish the defendant for the violation but rather to sanction the breach of trust inherent in violating release conditions, limiting the sentencing court's considerations accordingly.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the initial Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit holds it belongs to the estate, while other circuits hold it belongs to the debtor, based on differing readings of § 348(f)(1)(A) and § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), coupled with the broad scope of § 541(a), means that post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code as a whole establishes that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor, consistent with § 348(f)'s purpose of encouraging good-faith Chapter 13 filings without penalizing debtors who must later convert.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to appeals from orders denying attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment.
splits.description: Circuits have split on whether a motion for attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to the civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case itself (subject to the criminal appeal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, and thus the civil appeal deadline (30 days under FRAP 4(a)) applies rather than the criminal deadline.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is part of the criminal proceedings and thus the criminal appeal deadline (14 days under FRAP 4(b)) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal medical records in litigation is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine as an order involving a value of 'high order' that is effectively unreviewable after final judgment.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denials of motions to seal documents referencing medical treatments and diagnoses are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order.' Other circuits have taken varying approaches to when sealing denials qualify for collateral order review.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that medical privacy is a value of such high order that denial of a motion to seal medical records is effectively unreviewable after final judgment, satisfying the collateral order doctrine for immediate appeal.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denials of motions to seal do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine because the privacy interest, while important, can be adequately vindicated through other means or on appeal from final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether legal errors or constitutional claims that could have been raised in a § 2255 habeas petition may also serve as the basis for compassionate release. Some circuits permit courts to consider such claims as one factor, while others hold that compassionate release cannot be used as a substitute for habeas review.

positions.label: May consider conviction-related errors
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: May not use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A) may not be used as a vehicle to challenge the validity of a conviction or sentence, as those claims must be raised through § 2255 habeas proceedings.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under 42 U.S.C. § 1981 or analogous federal law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits about the standards for discrimination claims in business and hospitality settings. The Second Circuit's approach was found sufficiently unsettled to warrant review, suggesting a circuit split on the applicable legal framework for liability and damages.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Applies a more plaintiff-friendly standard for establishing discrimination claims in hospitality or business settings, allowing claims to proceed with less direct evidence of discriminatory intent.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies a more restrictive standard for discrimination claims in business establishments, requiring stronger evidence of intentional discrimination.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which bars states from enacting or enforcing laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any . . . broker,' preempts state negligence claims arising from a freight broker's selection of a motor carrier. This question affects liability in the trucking industry where brokers play a significant intermediary role.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted because they relate to the broker's 'service' of arranging transportation, which falls within the FAAAA's preemption clause.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers for negligent hiring of motor carriers are not preempted because they do not directly regulate brokers' prices, routes, or services within the meaning of the FAAAA.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to a person who uses marijuana.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass'n v. Bruen, circuits have split on whether the federal prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users — particularly marijuana users — is consistent with the Second Amendment's text and historical tradition of firearms regulation.

positions.label: § 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) does not violate the Second Amendment because the historical tradition of firearms regulation supports disarming individuals whose drug use renders them dangerous or irresponsible.

positions.label: § 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a sufficient historical analogue justifying the disarmament of non-violent drug users.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the Section 1 exemption for transportation workers, particularly whether last-mile delivery workers who distribute goods to retail stores are 'engaged in . . . interstate commerce.' This affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a wide range of distribution workers.

positions.label: Broad exemption — last-mile delivery workers qualify
positions.summary: Holds that workers who are part of a continuous interstate transportation chain, including those making last-mile deliveries of goods that have moved in interstate commerce, qualify as transportation workers exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow exemption — last-mile distributors do not qualify
positions.summary: Holds that distribution workers delivering goods locally to retail stores are not 'transportation workers engaged in . . . interstate commerce' under Section 1 because they are not themselves moving goods across state lines.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claims are based on labeling that the EPA approved. This affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticides nationwide.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would require labeling different from or in addition to what the EPA has approved.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because they impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements, consistent with the Supreme Court's Bates v. Dow Agrosciences framework.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
